story_text.value:
I've been working on this project for a few years, and thinking about it for a few more years. Ever since the pandemic when I did my entire job on a little Chromebook with browser-based tools; why not make an Audacity for the browser?

Well, it turned out there were already a few "Audacities for the Browser" like https://audiomass.co/ (posted here a couple times already), https://naomiaro.com/waveform-playlist/, and a literal Audacity compiled to WebAssembly https://wavacity.com/. SoundEtch is kind of a beefed up version of those.

I made it with podcasters and other spoken-word creators in mind, rather than musicians, since there are a number of browser DAWs already e.g. OpenDAW.

Everything is streamed to and from disk (OPFS), with an optional cloud backup. You can close or crash the browser tab, even in the middle of recording, and your data is still there when you open it back up. This also means you can load huge files; my parents' desktop with 8gb RAM handled this 5 hour stereo mp3 I found on archive https://archive.org/details/2023-09-08/2023-09-10.mp3.

There's a transcription-based editing tool like you get with Riverside and Descript. Mine uses IBM's Granite Turbo model, plus some Codex/Claude tweaking to get word-level timestamps. The result is, to my knowledge, much faster and more accurate than any other browser/local ASR out there. It has a few quirks, though, like only emitting lower-case letters and spaces.

I also added a WebRTC meeting room with up to 4 guests. It doesn't have a TURN service, so some networks will block you from connecting.

Since AI coding assistants are so good these days, I was able to add video support pretty easily. You can import, export, and record video, add that transcript with the current word highlighted, etc.

The editing is pretty basic for now: you can trim the clips, move them around, add some effects including noise removal from DeepFilterNet (https://github.com/Rikorose/DeepFilterNet).

I appreciate your taking a look and any feedback you have! The code is at https://github.com/bfbsoundetch/SoundEtch

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I built a mutation testing tool that takes a different approach from the conventional one. I'm calling it Targeted Mutation Testing.

As AI coding has become more common, mutation testing has become more important. It has helped me a lot personally. But ever since I first learned about it, I've kept wondering if there was a smarter way to do it.

Targeted Mutation Testing observes a single test run and generates targeted mutants from what it sees.

Of course, observation-guided rules have their own limits, so you can also combine them with classic mutation rules when you want more coverage.

This post links to the Rust implementation, which I built first. I also built a JS/TS implementation:

https://github.com/t-k/targeted-mutation-ts

What's interesting about the JS/TS version is that, by focusing on targeted mutants, mutation testing can become practical for E2E tests.

I took inspiration from SEMu, DSpot, the W-method, and Meta's ACH. I listed the links at the end.

Would love any feedback. Thanks for taking a look.

- Killing Stubborn Mutants with Symbolic Execution (SEMu): https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.02941

- Automatic Test Improvement with DSpot: https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.08330

- Testing Software Design Modeled by Finite-State Machines (W-method): https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.1978.231496

- Mutation-Guided LLM-based Test Generation at Meta (ACH): https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12862

story_text.value:
Dualayer Hierarchy Standard (DHS:

Repo: https://github.com/Zainium-Dynamics/dualayer-hierarchy-stand... Full Specification (23-page PDF): https://zainiumdynamics.tech/dhs

DHS 1.1 defines a layered filesystem hierarchy for immutable Linux systems where musl and glibc coexist side by side without conflict. Either C library can be primary; the distribution chooses.

Root layout (no /usr, /bin, /sbin, /lib, /lib64, /etc, /var, or /boot at /, not even as symlinks):

  /
  |-- overlayer/   (the entire OS: all layers)
  |-- home/        (user home directories)
  |-- root/        (root home)
  |-- dev/         (devtmpfs)
  |-- proc/        (procfs)
  |-- sys/         (sysfs)
  |-- run/         (tmpfs; removable media at /run/media/user/label)
  `-- tmp/         (temporary files)
Layer structure under /overlayer (composed at boot via OverlayFS with syshub as lower and userland/union as upper):

  /overlayer/
  |-- syshub/           (read-only base OS; boots without userland)
  |-- userland/         (installed packages: union/, work/, registry/)
  |-- ignition/         (kernels, initramfs, bootloader; read-only)
  |-- agents/           (optional AI coding agent instructions/policies)
  `-- .syshub-pending/  (staged atomic base upgrade, applied at next boot)
Dual-libc isolation: musl and glibc each live in their own GNU target-triplet directory (arch-vendor-linux-musl and arch-vendor-linux-gnu) with separate loaders, headers, C++ runtimes, loader configs, and toolchains. Shared directories (/overlayer/syshub/bin, lib, include) belong strictly to the primary libc and search paths never cross, while both read shared system config (passwd, hosts, resolv.conf, zoneinfo) from /overlayer/syshub/etc.

FHS compatibility: Foreign packages are adapted at install time (PT_INTERP, RPATH, pkg-config, shebangs). Runtime FHS path lookups use a preload resolver and loader redirection (the known LD_PRELOAD limitation for static/setuid binaries is documented in Chapter 7).

Reference implementation — Zainium OS (https://github.com/Zainium-Dynamics): - Layers: syshub (base), zexlib (userland), zaisys (ignition) - Libc design: Design A (musl primary in base, glibc as a userland package) - Boot & atomic upgrades: quantra-ramfs - Package manager & receipts: zex - Path/loader resolver & toolchain switcher: libsys_resolver.so, sys-resolver - Protected base/ignition paths: elevate, elevate-pam

Looking for honest technical critique on where this layout holds up, where it breaks down, and what edge cases are missing.

story_text.value:
In 2020, I wrote Rocketcrab, a lobby service and launcher for mobile web party games. (Hacker News post from 2020: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=24876148)

You would create a "party," which gave you a URL like rocketcrab.com/abcd that you could send to your friends. You could choose from a library of games, and those games would be shown on everyone's devices via iframe.

The site was fairly successful, probably mostly because I forced all the users of my game Drawphone (https://rocketcrab.com/game/drawphone) to play it via Rocketcrab. ;D But over the years, I lost interest in maintaining Rocketcrab. People are still playing, though, so I kept paying the $12/month for the server!

Recently, with the new AI coding agents, I was inspired to bring two ideas to life in Rocketcrab: make-your-own vibe-coded games and serverless multiplayer.

The vibe-coded games feature is called Nova: you copy a prompt into your favorite AI, work with it to build a game, and paste the resulting one-shot HTML back into Rocketcrab. No login needed! The HTML is stored only in your browser and is sent to your friends via iframe when playing together.

For serverless multiplayer, I used the awesome open-source P2P library Trystero (https://trystero.dev/), with some Cloudflare Durable Objects and fallback TURN for strict enterprise networks.

Rocketcrab is 100% free and open-source under the MIT license. The rewrite was done mostly with Opus 5.5 and GPT 6.2 Sol, plus a security audit with Gemini 4 Neon.

Feel free to send me any ideas or feedback, or open issues and pull requests on GitHub: https://github.com/tannerkrewson/rocketcrab

I just cut over to the rewrite a few hours ago, so let me know if there are any issues! I'm planning to add some new games I've found on the web to the library, just as soon as my five-hour Claude window resets. :D

PS: You've got about a day left to build a Nova game and try it with your family tomorrow... happy thanksgiving!
